text: Hongkong, Tuesday, March 16, 1926.

label: paragraph_title
text: SHAREHOLDERS' APATHY.

label: text
text: Anyone who has had experience of company meetings either in Hongkong or elsewhere in the East cannot but be in full accord with the "disgust", expressed at yesterday's meeting of the Telephone Company in regard to the poor attendance of shareholders. Mr. D. McNeill, who aired the grievance, expressed surprise that both in that and other companies with which he is connected the shareholders take no apparent interest in their own financial affairs—they are content to read the reports in the newspapers and then proceed to "chew the rag" as to the best way of improving affairs. They are satisfied to argue, instead of attending meetings and putting their views before the directors.

label: text
text: The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak made the only rejoinder possible. The directors sympathised with Mr. McNeill in his views and he felt sure that the directors of any company would welcome criticism which was fair, and which was constructive and not destructive. Directors would welcome helpful criticism in preference to having shareholders whispering behind their backs.

label: text
text: There is no suggestion, of course, that in regard to the Telephone Company in particular there has been any whisperings behind the backs of the directors. It was a mere generalisation in regard to the attitude of shareholders of any company toward those whom they appoint as directors of their own affairs. If the cap fits any individual shareholder of any company or any clique of shareholders then, of course, they are welcome to try it on. Still, it is not "cricket" in the commercial world. If directors are worthy of the position to which they are elected they are entitled to receive the co-operation of shareholders—to be told the good as well as the bad and to be the receptacle of that kind of criticism that is based on the true interests of that particular company in which they themselves have a pecuniary interest. Even destructive criticism, if advanced in the proper spirit, can often be useful to directors, and it is certainly not to be discounted so long as it is expressed at meetings of shareholders and not behind the backs of directors. Time and again in the history

label: text
text: a quorum at shareholders' meetings has outrivalled Japhet's famous search for a father: Even the anticipated announcement of a dividend has failed to secure the attendance of shareholders. But there is apparently no remedy for this state of affairs. Perhaps Mr. McNeill, who initiated the discussion on the point yesterday, would like to take a leaf out of the book of Trade Unions and impose a nominal fine on those shareholders who fail to attend duly convened meetings. Compulsory interest of this kind would not, however, be very helpful toward the proper conduct of the company's affairs; and, after all, if shareholders cannot voluntarily be induced to attend to watch their own interests, then not all the protests of surprise and disgust will do any good. And there is this to be said—so long as the affairs of the company are being administered as they ought to be, the absence of shareholders may often be construed as a graceful compliment to the directors. Conversely, let one word be whispered that all is not well, and shareholders' meetings will be packed. Which, again, has been a common experience both in Hongkong and elsewhere.

label: paragraph_title
text: STREET FOUNTAINS.

label: text
text: The poetic fancy of newspaper reporters which dubs these public water-taps, street fountains, is to be encouraged. A tap by any other name would still waste as much water, and help sear the tempers of the many who wait patiently their turn for a supply of “nature's ale” and who oft dispute for pride of place. Is there a saving of water in the method adopted when a famine seems imminent? Presumably there must be otherwise it would not be put into operation—or some other method would be attempted. Doubts arise when the spectacle of ever-flowing "fountains" is noticed with numbers around them—some in the early, intermediate, and concluding stages, either of personal ablutions, or more often than not—in that of considerable cleansing of clothes. The flow of water is generally at full strength, and the amount that finds its way into gutters on the way to smelly sewers is great indeed. This is not all. A big waste of water is occasioned by defective fittings, which produce, not merely the drops that are like mercy, but the steady flow that prevails throughout each successive twenty-four hours of the day. A saving of water would be made if the Chinese equivalent of the English plumber could be sent round periodically to inspect "fountains," to re-washer them where necessary, and to reduce the waste of water occasioned by defective fittings, to the minimum. The insistence of the queue and its fairness has demonstrated itself to the Chinese, and it is the best in the circumstances. If it is the early bird that gets the worm, it is the early attender at street fountains who gets the first or earliest supply of water. But is there any rule as to the supply which may be taken at one time? It may be over-sagerless in the

label: text
text: direction of getting large supplies which leads to disturbances at the fountains, — often to cracked heads. These disturbances should be frowned upon by the authorities, and guilty parties dealt with as severely as possible. Whether it is worth while preaching lessons on the iniquity of wasting water we know not. There are numbers of Chinese of the frame of mind of Mr. G. K. label: doc_title
text: ARMY NEEDS.

label: text
text: SEARCH FOR A MECHANICAL

label: text
text: PROMOTION PROBLEMS

label: text
text: (British Wireless Service.)

label: text
text: In introducing the Army Estimates for 1926-7 in, the House of Commons Sir Laming. Worthington Evans, Secretary of State for War, said that it had not been easy to secure a reduction of 32,000,000, which the Estimates showed, as compared with those for the current year. The total net amount he was asking for was £42,500,000 compared with £44,500,000 in the current year. He pointed out that in 1921 the Army expenditure was £88,000,000 or twice the amount of the Estimates now submitted. Even of the £42,500,000 which he asked for nearly £8,000,000 would go to retired pay and pensions.

label: paragraph_title
text: "Mechanicalisation"

label: text
text:
The Minister said that the manoeuvres of last Autumn had taught important lessons in regard to the use of mechanical vehicles. It was shown that the necessary mobility could not be achieved if horse transport accompanied mechanically moved troops. Until, however, a satisfactory type of machine could be evolved, which also had commercial possibilities, the cost of mechanicalising large forces would prove prohibitive.
Research and experiment were continuing with a view to evolving something which could be of general, as well as military, use, and which commercial users would stock, so that it would be available in large numbers in case of need. The extent, therefore, to which the field Army could be mechanicalised still remained in doubt.

label: text
text: It had been decided to approach the problem step by step. In the first instance they would form a small mechanical force of all arms for experimental purposes, and they would not attempt any large production of mechanical vehicles until they were certain that they had evolved the required type. They were, he was advised, already ahead of other nations in mechanicalisation, and there was, therefore, no justification for uneconomical haste.

label: paragraph_title
text: Greatest Asset.

label: text
text: Dealing with the promotion of officers, Sir L. Worthington Evans said that the Army Council was unanimously of the opinion that no change in the present system of normal promotion from Second Lieutenant to Major was either necessary or desirable, and that nothing should be done which would in any way impair the greatest asset which the British Army possessed, namely, regimental esprit de corps.

label: text
text:
The Army Council had, however, decided that in the junior ranks officers of marked ability should receive accelerated promotion.
Promotion, above the rank of Major would now be by rigid selection, increasing in severity as the higher ranks were reached. Above the rank of Lieutenant Colonel the selection would become still more drastic. It was hoped that by this means any officer of outstanding and proved merit would get his chance to reach the highest rank in the service.

label: paragraph_title
text: SENATOR BORAH'S BELATED RESOLUTION.

label: text
text: (Reuter's American Service.)

label: text
text: Washington, March 10. Senator Borah introduced a resolution in the Senate requesting the State Department to report what steps have been taken toward the negotiation of the American claims against Great Britain and France in connection with the alleged violation of the rights of neutrals prior to the American entry into the war. The resolution was referred to the Foreign Relations Committee, or which Senator Borah is Chairman.

label: paragraph_title
text: DAY'S LABOUR.

label: text
text: FIVE NATIONS REPRESENTED:

label: text
text: Minister, at the Ministry of Labour to-day opened the International Conference convened by the British Government to consider the possibility of an international agreement regulating the hours of labour.

label: text
text: Great Britain, France, Belgium, Germany and Italy are represented.

label: paragraph_title
text: SOCIAL PROGRESS.

label: paragraph_title
text: (British Wireless Service.)

label: text
text: In his address of welcome to the delegates to the International Conference on hours of labour, Mr. Baldwin said:

label: text
text: "We are all of us advanced countries and we enjoy the benefits of a high degree of social progress. Uniformity among ourselves may have far-reaching consequences to the civilisation of the whole of Europe. There are people who say that international labour regulations may be of more benefit to one country than to another. That is not so. There can be no question in Europe of any country attaining prosperity at the expense of another country. Each one of us can prosper best and can make the greatest progress in material wellbeing when prosperity is the common property of all countries and when progress can be made advancing together."

label: paragraph_title
text: "FLOWING GOLD."

label: text
text: THIRTY MILLION DOLLARS FROM CANADA.

label: text
text: BIGGEST SINCE AUTUMN

label: text
text: (Reuter's American Service.)

label: text
text: The arrival of thirty million dollars from Canada within the past fortnight marks the largest movement of gold to New York since the British shipment last autumn.

label: text
text: The remittance is not expected to be greatly increased as the Canadian rate of exchange, which originally induced the movement of gold, has been steadily improving, during the past few days.

label: paragraph_title
text: FLIGHTY FRANCS.

label: paragraph_title
text:
LONDON MONEY MARKET
PUZZLED

label: text
text:
The French and Belgian francs in London closed, respectively, at 134.75 1/16 and 116.87.
The Belgian francs have previously slumped to 121.50 after being steady about 107 for a year.

label: text
text: The slump is attributed to a cessation of Belgian Government support as the result of a hitch in the negotiations in London and New York to advance credits to Belgium.

label: paragraph_title
text: Bankors' Demand.

label: text
text: The "Soir" says that the Minister of Finance declares that the Banks have fully assented to the measures to meet the situation, and from tomorrow exchange will be properly supported.

label: text
text:
The measures contemplated will prevent speculation, and control of the Exchanges will be reinforced.
The Minister of Finance made a statement at a meeting of the Cabinet regarding negotiations with the London bankers, who are demanding control over the Belgian railways in connection with the desired loan, according to a newspaper report from Paris.

label: paragraph_title
text: 3Y-ELECTION FOR ENGLISH UNIVERSITIES

label: paragraph_title
text: (Router's Service.)

label: paragraph_title
text: London, March 15.

label: text
text: The Government has gained a seat at the by-election for the English Universities due to the resignation of Mr. H. A. L. Fisher (formerly Minister of Education and a Liberal).

label: text
text: The candidates were Sir Arthur Hopkinson, Conservative, who was M.P. for the Crickdale Division of Wilts from 1895 to 1898; and Mr. Ramsay Muir, Liberal Editor of the Weekly Westminster, who was M.P. for Rochdale from 1923 until the General Election in October, 1924, when he was ousted by Mr. M. T. Kelly, Labourite, as the result of a triangular contest.

label: text
text: The polling for the English Universities was declared to-day as follows:—

label: text
text:
Hopkinson (Conservative).....2,343
Muir (Liberal).....2,000

label: text
text: The combined Universities of Durham, Manchester, Liverpool, Leeds, Sheffield, Birmingham and Bristol return two members to the House of Commons. The result at last General Election was:

label: text
text:

Mr. H. A. L. Fisher, Lib......2,064

label: paragraph_title
text: LONDON STRIKE

label: text
text: INIONS DECISION REJECTED BY MEN.

label: paragraph_title
text: London, March 15.

label: text
text: A mass meeting of workers at Messrs. R. Hoe & Co.'s factory decided not to accept the decision of the National Committee of the Amalgamated Engineering Union, and declined to resume work.

label: text
text: [The previous message relative to this strike, dated March 10, read:—A lively mass meeting of Messrs. Hoe's strikers' rejected a recommendation of the Executives of the Unions to return to work and resolved not to resume until non-Unionists have been removed and a substantial increase in wages assured. The Executives have called a meeting to consider disciplinary action. As a result of a meeting of the members of the Executives of the seven Unions concerned with the dispute at Hoe's factory and Sir Allan Smith, Chairman of the Employers' Federation, the employers have agreed to defer the operation of lock out notices until March 18.]

label: paragraph_title
text: TRAIN DERAILED.

label: paragraph_title
text:
FIFTY FEET PLUNGE
INTO RIVER.

label: text
text: HEAVY DEATH ROLL.

label: text
text: (Reuter's American Service.)

label: text
text: According to advices from the railway owners, 178 persons were killed and 75 others injured in the derailment of an excursion train, near San Jose, Costa Rica.

label: text
text: Three coaches left the rails and plunged fifty feet from the embankment into the river.

label: text
text:
New York, March 15.
The casualty roll in the Costa Rica accident is now stated to be 248 killed and 93 injured.

label: text
text: Three coaches were demolished; of which one fell into the river from the bridge, and the others hung from a precipice 190 feet high.

label: text
text: There were 1,000 passengers on the train. The object of the excursion was to raise funds for a charitable purpose.

label: text
text: Three days' public mourning has been ordered.

label: paragraph_title
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: The Belgian airman, Lieut. Mndaets, has left for Ansouan.

label: text
text: The Belgian airmen flying to the Congo have arrived at Athara.

label: text
text: [A Brussels cable of March 9 reported: The Belgian airmen, Medaets and Verhaegen, with the mechanic Coppens left at seven o'clock this morning for Belgrade, in an attempt to fly to the Belgian Congo via Cairo and the Nile]
